questions.q: Using this lesson's blueprint analogy, what is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class and an object are two different names for the exact same thing
An object defines the behavior, and a class stores the actual data values
A class is the blueprint defining fields and behavior; an object is a specific instance built from that blueprint, with its own concrete field values
A class can only ever produce exactly one object
questions.explain: The lesson's analogy is explicit: one blueprint (class) can produce many houses (objects), each with the same structure but its own concrete details -- here, its own field values.

questions.q: In the Customer class example, why does calling `c1.addPoints(50)` have zero effect on `c2.loyaltyPoints`?
options: Because c1 and c2 are two completely separate objects, each carrying its own independent copy of the class's fields
Because addPoints is a static method shared by all Customer objects
Because Apex automatically synchronizes loyaltyPoints across every Customer object
Because addPoints always resets loyaltyPoints to zero
questions.explain: The lesson explains that c1 and c2 are separate objects with independent field values, so an instance method called on one object only ever affects that object's own data, never another object's.

questions.q: What is a constructor, per this lesson?
options: A method that can only return a Boolean value
A keyword used only inside static methods
A field that stores the number of objects created so far
A special method, matching the class's own name, with no return type, that runs automatically when a new object is created and sets up its initial field values
questions.explain: The lesson defines the constructor as a special method sharing the class's name, with no return type, that runs automatically on object creation to set up initial field values -- the Customer(String customerName) method in the example.

questions.q: What is the rule of thumb this lesson gives for choosing between an instance method and a static method?
options: Always use static methods, since instance methods are deprecated
If a method needs a specific object's own data to do its job, make it an instance method; if it's a general-purpose operation independent of any one object's state, a static method is simpler
Instance methods can only be used inside constructors
Static methods require creating an object first, while instance methods do not
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb ties the choice directly to whether the method needs a specific object's own data (instance method) or not (static method, which doesn't require creating an object first).

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the Salesforce-specific wrinkle around the word 'object'?
options: A 'Salesforce object' (like Account or Opportunity) refers to a data structure in the Salesforce database, closer to what a general class represents, not an instance of one -- a different, equally legitimate use of the same word
Salesforce never uses the word 'object' at all
In Salesforce, 'object' and 'class' are always perfectly interchangeable with no distinction
Salesforce objects can never have fields
questions.explain: The lesson flags that Salesforce's own usage of 'object' (an Account or Opportunity object) is closer to what a general programming class represents, not an instance -- a distinct but equally valid meaning from the general programming-object meaning this lesson otherwise teaches.
